overviewHtml:
This ungraded knowledge check assesses your understanding of Husserl's methods for suspending the natural attitude. You'll be asked about the natural attitude, the difference between the epoché and Cartesian doubt, the aim of the reduction, the steps of free variation, and transcendental idealism.

Note: Use this to test yourself, review the feedback on any questions you miss, and retry until you feel confident before moving forward.

forms.stemHtml: Husserl calls the standing belief that the world exists the of the .

options.html: general thesis
options.text: general thesis
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The general thesis is the constant, unspoken belief that the world exists as actuality.

options.html: epoché
options.text: epoché
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The epoché suspends the belief in the world's existence. The belief itself is the general thesis.

options.html: reduction
options.text: reduction
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The reduction leads attention back to givenness. The belief in the world's existence is the general thesis.

options.html: natural attitude
options.text: natural attitude
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The general thesis runs through the natural attitude, the ordinary stance in which the world is simply there.

options.html: eidetic science
options.text: eidetic science
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Eidetic science studies essences. The belief in the world's existence belongs to the natural attitude.

options.html: transcendental idealism
options.text: transcendental idealism
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Transcendental idealism is a conclusion Husserl drew from the reduction. The belief in the world's existence belongs to the natural attitude.

forms.stemHtml: How does the epoché differ from Cartesian doubt?

options.html: The epoché denies that the world exists, while doubt only questions it
options.text: The epoché denies that the world exists, while doubt only questions it
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The epoché doesn't deny the world. It suspends the belief in the world's existence without affirming, denying, or doubting it.

options.html: The epoché suspends the belief without doubting or denying it
options.text: The epoché suspends the belief without doubting or denying it
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Doubt takes up a new attitude toward the belief. The epoché leaves the belief as it is and makes no use of it, so that attention can turn to how things are given.

options.html: The epoché doubts only the sciences, not everyday perception
options.text: The epoché doubts only the sciences, not everyday perception
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The epoché doesn't doubt anything. It suspends the belief in the world's existence, together with the sciences that rest on it.

options.html: The epoché and doubt are two names for the same method
options.text: The epoché and doubt are two names for the same method
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Husserl distinguishes them. The epoché suspends the belief without doubting or denying it.

forms.stemHtml: What is the aim of the phenomenological reduction?

options.html: To prove that the world depends on the mind for its existence
options.text: To prove that the world depends on the mind for its existence
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Husserl drew transcendental idealism from the reduction, but the reduction's aim is to lead attention back from objects to their givenness in consciousness.

options.html: To reduce mental states to their neural causes in the brain
options.text: To reduce mental states to their neural causes in the brain
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. That would be a causal reduction. The phenomenological reduction leads attention back from objects to their givenness in consciousness.

options.html: To lead attention back from objects to their givenness
options.text: To lead attention back from objects to their givenness
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The reduction, from the Latin reducere, "to lead back," turns attention from objects taken simply as existing to the ways they're given in experience.

options.html: To reduce experience to its simplest sensory elements
options.text: To reduce experience to its simplest sensory elements
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. That was the aim of introspective psychology. The phenomenological reduction leads attention back from objects to their givenness.

forms.stemHtml: Which of the following are steps in free variation? (Select all that apply.)

options.html: Start from an actual or imagined example
options.text: Start from an actual or imagined example
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Free variation begins with an example of the kind you want to understand.

options.html: Vary the example's features freely in imagination
options.text: Vary the example's features freely in imagination
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! You change features such as color, size, and viewpoint in imagination.

options.html: Count how often each feature appears across many real cases
options.text: Count how often each feature appears across many real cases
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Free variation doesn't count cases. That would be empirical generalization. It finds what can't be removed.

options.html: Note which features can't be removed without changing the kind
options.text: Note which features can't be removed without changing the kind
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Features that survive every variation belong to the essence.

forms.stemHtml: What did Husserl's transcendental idealism claim, on the reading presented here?

options.html: The world is a mental image that exists only while perceived
options.text: The world is a mental image that exists only while perceived
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Husserl didn't claim the world is a mental image. His transcendental idealism holds that the world's being is being-for-consciousness, so what existence means is clarified by how it's given.

options.html: The world exists entirely independently of any possible experience
options.text: The world exists entirely independently of any possible experience
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. That's closer to realism. Husserl's transcendental idealism holds that the world's being is being-for-consciousness.

options.html: The world's being is being-for-consciousness, clarified by its givenness
options.text: The world's being is being-for-consciousness, clarified by its givenness
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Husserl held that what it means for something to exist is clarified by how existence is given in experience. Whether this is metaphysical idealism remains debated.

options.html: The world can be known only through the natural sciences
options.text: The world can be known only through the natural sciences
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The epoché puts the sciences out of action. Husserl's transcendental idealism holds that the world's being is being-for-consciousness.

title: Epoché, Reduction, and Variation
